cases.case_text:
A 76-year-old woman presented with macular edema. The patient was treated with 2 intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injections. At 3 months after presentation, her macular edema was completely resolved, without recurrence.

No specific physical examination findings were reported in the case.

- Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA) findings:    At 6 months: No abnormality observed    At 12 months: En face OCT revealed hyperreflective tissues starting to proliferate on retinal vessels; OCTA B-scan showed pyramid-shaped proliferations    At 15 months: Hyperreflective tissues increased in size with angiogenic sprouts showing flow signals extending vertically    At 18 months: Development observed in area of preexisting proliferation    At 21 months: Enlarged horizontal structures along retina surface  - Fluorescein Angiography:    Performed at 21 months showing dendritic vascular-like structures  Image Descriptions:  Figure 1: Sequential development over 1 year showing progression from normal vessels to proliferation  Figure 2: Multimodal images at 21 months showing enlarged neovascularization

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A. Retinal Vein Occlusion with Neovascularization
B. Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
C. Branch retinal vein occlusion with secondary neovascularization
D. Branch retinal vein occlusion with preretinal neovascularization

source_options.C: Juvenile spring eruption (JSE) associated with parvovirus B19 infection

cases.case_text:
A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

Erythema and helical thickening as well as numerous small blisters, 2 to 3 mm in diameter, were present on both ears. Similar vesicles were observed at the upper and lower vermillion border. Several erythematous papules and crusts were located on the cheeks, neck, and lower arms.

- Laboratory tests: Differential blood count, routine chemical analysis, and serum porphyrins were unremarkable. Serum parvovirus B19 (PVB19) IgM and IgG antibodies were detectable. Bacterial cultures from blister fluid were unremarkable.- Virologic analyses: Negative results for herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, varicella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpesvirus 6, hepatitis B and C viruses, 8 human polyomaviruses, and enteroviruses. PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Polymorphous light eruption
B. Polymorphic light eruption
C. Juvenile spring eruption (JSE) associated with parvovirus B19 infection
D. Parvovirus B19-associated photodermatitis

cases.case_text:
A man in his 40s, weighing 109kg, with stage IV KRAS wild-type rectal adenocarcinoma diagnosed in November 2013. He had pulmonary and liver metastases. His treatment history included radiation therapy and multiple chemotherapy cycles. In December 2014, he was enrolled in trial E7208 at the Smilow Cancer Hospital at Yale-New Haven and was randomized to receive combination therapy every 2 weeks.

In early January 2015, the patient developed a single, well-defined, blanchable bright red plaque densely composed of telangiectasias on his lower right lateral shin, which grew to 4 cm. The lesion was not associated with pain or pruritus.

source_options.A: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified

cases.case_text:
A man in his 50s presented with pink-purple dermal papules and polyarticular inflammatory arthritis involving the wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, and proximal interphalangeal joints. He experienced fatigue, dyspnea on exertion, and reported a 5-7 kg weight loss without fever or sweats. His pulmonary and joint symptoms were relieved by daily oral prednisone and flared with taper below 10 mg. Previous treatments included hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily for 18 months and weekly adalimumab injections for 7 months, without improvement.

Numerous pink-purple dermal papules were present on the trunk and extremities, with preference for the extensor surfaces of the arms and legs. No lymphadenopathy was noted.

- Laboratory tests: Complete blood cell count, metabolic panel, hemoglobin A1c, viral and rheumatologic panels (including HIV), and serum/urine protein electrophoresis were normal or unremarkable.- Imaging studies:  - Chest radiograph: Normal  - High-resolution chest CT scan: Unremarkable  - Hand radiographs: Normal  - Echocardiography: Normal- Pulmonary Function Tests: Revealed mild restrictive disease with decreased forced vital capacity and total lung capacity- Pathology:  Image Title: Skin Biopsy Findings  Image Description: A) Pink-purple papules on extensor surface of arms  B) Nodular to diffuse lymphohistiocytic infiltrate (H&E stain)  C) Admixed atypical, irregularly contoured lymphocytes with numerous histiocytes  D) Low CD4 signal and robust CD8 signal (20x magnification)- Additional Testing:  - T-cell receptor PCR: Matching clonal rearrangements identified in 3 skin biopsy specimens and bone marrow sample  - Flow cytometry of bone marrow: Revealed lymphocytes with atypical CD3-negative, CD4-negative, CD5-positive, CD8-positive phenotype (2% of total cells)  - Immunostaining: Lymphocytes positive for CD3, inverted CD8:CD4 ratio, predominantly α/β positive

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Peripheral T-cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified
B. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, CD8+ variant
C. Mycosis fungoides (CD8-predominant variant)
D. CD8-positive granulomatous cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
